problems.title: Fighter turn fight: corner speed against the sustained turn
problems.setup: A fighter at 6000 m (ISA ρ = 0.660 kg/m³) weighs W = 150 kN with S = 40 m², combat C_Lmax = 1.2 and positive limit load factor n_max = 7.5. Polar C_D = 0.020 + 0.10C_L². Available thrust at this altitude is T = 90 kN, taken constant with speed. Level turns, g = 9.81 m/s².

parts.ask: Find the corner speed (true airspeed) at 6000 m.
sol: Corner: stall line meets n_max, n_max·W = ½ρV²SC_Lmax

parts.ask: Find the instantaneous turn rate at the corner, in deg/s.
sol: ω = 15.7 deg/s, the peak turn rate on the whole envelope

parts.ask: At the same speed, find the highest load factor the fighter can sustain (thrust equals drag).
sol: T = qS(C_D0 + K(nW/(qS))²) gives n² = (q/(K·W/S))(T/W − qC_D0/(W/S))

parts.ask: The pilot pulls the full 7.5 g at the corner anyway. Find the specific excess power P_s.
sol: P_s = V(T − D)/W = 266.5·(90 − 153.8)/150 = −113 m/s: the jet bleeds energy

parts.ask: Examiner twist: the same fight at sea level, same weight. How do corner speed and the turn rate at the corner change?
parts.a: Corner speed in TAS drops to about 196 m/s (same EAS) and the turn rate at the corner rises to about 21 deg/s
w: Corner speed stays at 266.5 m/s TAS and the turn rate stays at 15.7 deg/s
Corner speed rises by √(1.225/0.660) and the turn rate falls
Corner speed drops to about 196 m/s and the turn rate stays at 15.7 deg/s, since n_max is the same
sol: V* ∝ 1/√ρ at fixed W/S, C_Lmax and n_max: 266.5·√(0.660/1.225) = 195.6 m/s
Same n at lower V: ω = 9.81·7.43/195.6 = 0.373 rad/s = 21.4 deg/s

problems.x: Corner speed gives the best instantaneous turn, while thrust sets the sustained turn, and the gap between them is paid for in negative specific excess power.

problems.title: Supersonic airliner wave drag and the area rule
problems.setup: A supersonic airliner cruises at M = 1.6 at 15 km (p = 12,040 Pa, γ = 1.4). Its total cross-sectional area distribution has maximum A_max = 8 m² over an overall length l = 50 m. Wing reference area S = 120 m². Use the Sears-Haack ideal D/q = (9π/2)(A_max/l)², and an empirical efficiency factor E_WD = 1.8 for the real shape: D_wave/q = E_WD·(9π/2)(A_max/l)².

parts.ask: Supersonic area ruling uses oblique cuts at the Mach angle. Find the Mach angle μ.
sol: μ = 38.7°: cut the body with planes tilted at μ and average around the roll angle

parts.ask: Find the wave drag force at cruise, in kN.
Express the wave drag as a drag coefficient on S, in drag counts (1 count = 0.0001).
sol: 54 counts, about a third of a typical subsonic transport C_D0

parts.ask: What does the area rule tell the designer to do at the wing root?
parts.a: Waist the fuselage where the wing joins, so the total area A(x) of fuselage plus wing follows one smooth Sears-Haack shape
w: Shape the fuselage alone as a Sears-Haack body and add the wing area on top of it
Raise A_max with a fatter fuselage so the nose and tail are more gradual
Keep the fuselage cross-section constant over the wing root chord
sol: Far-field wave drag depends on the total A(x) and its second derivative
The wing adds a bump to A(x); removing the same area from the fuselage restores a smooth curve

parts.ask: Examiner twist: the total volume is fixed, but the designers stretch the airplane to l = 60 m (same Sears-Haack type shape and E_WD). Find the new wave drag.
sol: With fixed volume V, Sears-Haack D/q = 128V²/(πl⁴), so D ∝ 1/l⁴
A_max shrinks as V/l, which adds a second factor (50/60)² to the (50/60)² from 1/l²

problems.x: Wave drag scales with (A_max/l)² and with the smoothness of the total area distribution, so slender bodies and a waisted fuselage pay off at supersonic cruise.

problems.title: Battery commuter range against the Breguet fuel range
problems.setup: A nine seat electric commuter has mass m = 5000 kg, of which the battery is 1500 kg (battery mass fraction 0.30). Pack specific energy e* = 250 Wh/kg with 80% usable. Motor and inverter efficiency 0.90, propeller efficiency η_p = 0.80. Cruise L/D = 16 (wing S = 25 m², C_D = 0.025 + 0.039C_L²). The battery weight stays constant all flight. g = 9.81 m/s².

parts.ask: Find the electric cruise range on the usable energy.
sol: Energy to thrust = drag × distance at constant W: e*·f·η_m·η_p·m_b = (W/(L/D))·R

parts.ask: The same airframe burns fuel instead: 1500 kg of fuel (43 MJ/kg) in an engine of thermal efficiency 0.35, same η_p and L/D. Find the Breguet range.
Why does the electric range carry a linear mass fraction while Breguet carries a logarithm?
parts.a: The battery stays aboard, so the drag is set by the full weight for the whole flight; Breguet integrates over a falling weight, which gives ln(W_i/W_f)
w: The electric motor efficiency changes with state of charge, which removes the logarithm
Breguet assumes constant altitude while the electric equation assumes constant C_L
Battery specific energy rises as it discharges, which cancels the weight change
sol: dR = η(L/D)dE/W with W constant integrates to a linear form
With fuel, dW = −dE/e_f and ∫dW/W gives the logarithm

parts.ask: Find the best range speed for the electric version at 3000 m (ρ = 0.909 kg/m³).
sol: Constant weight, energy per distance ∝ drag, so fly at (L/D)_max like a propeller aircraft

parts.ask: Examiner twist: what pack specific energy would match the 7004 km fuel range with the same 30% battery fraction?
sol: Electric range is linear in e*: R_fuel/R_elec = 7004/253.7 = 27.6
e* = 250·27.6 = 6900 Wh/kg, about 28 times today's packs

problems.x: Electric range is linear in battery specific energy and mass fraction at constant weight, and it is flown at (L/D)_max like a propeller aircraft.

problems.title: Pull-up into a loop: the vertical-plane equations of motion
problems.setup: A jet trainer (W = 50 kN, g = 9.81 m/s²) flies wings level at V = 180 m/s and starts a pull-up into an inside loop, holding load factor n = L/W = 4. Point-mass equations in the vertical plane, thrust along the flight path, α small: m·dV/dt = T − D − W sin γ and m·V·dγ/dt = L − W cos γ.

parts.ask: At the start of the pull-up (γ = 0), find the radius of the flight path.
sol: mV²/R = L − W, so V²/(gR) = n − 1

parts.ask: Find the pitch rate of the flight path dγ/dt at that moment, in deg/s.
Passing γ = 60° the speed has fallen to 150 m/s, still at n = 4. Find dγ/dt.
sol: = 0.229 rad/s = 13.1 deg/s: the path tightens as cos γ falls and V falls

parts.ask: At γ = 60°, T − D = 5 kN. Find dV/dt.
sol: dV/dt = −7.51 m/s²: gravity along the path dominates

parts.ask: At constant n, where in the inside loop is the radius of the path smallest?
parts.a: At the top, where n − cos γ = n + 1 is largest and V is lowest
w: At the bottom, where the pilot feels the highest load factor
At γ = 90°, where gravity acts fully along the path
The radius is the same everywhere because n is held constant
sol: Top: cos γ = −1 and V is at its minimum, so both effects shrink R: the loop is egg shaped

problems.x: In the vertical plane, L − W cos γ turns the flight path and T − D − W sin γ changes the speed, so a constant-g loop tightens toward the top.

problems.title: STOL bush plane on a gravel strip, then on Venus
problems.setup: A STOL bush plane weighs W = 10 kN (mass 1019 kg) with S = 18 m² and full flap C_Lmax = 2.4. Sea level ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Liftoff at V_LO = 1.1V_stall. During the ground roll: average propeller thrust T = 3.0 kN, C_L = 0.5, C_D = 0.06, rolling friction μ = 0.08 on gravel. Use the mean acceleration evaluated at 0.7V_LO.

parts.ask: Find the liftoff speed.
Find the ground roll in still air.
Into an 8 m/s headwind, keeping the same mean acceleration, find the ground roll.
sol: s_G = 13.38²/(2·2.11) = 42.5 m: the roll scales with ground speed squared

parts.ask: The same airplane goes on floats for lake work. What shapes its water takeoff?
parts.a: Water resistance rises to a hump at an intermediate speed before the floats get up on the step and plane, so the thrust margin at the hump sets the takeoff
w: Water resistance is a constant friction coefficient times (W − L), like a runway
Water resistance falls steadily from zero speed, so the start of the run is the critical point
Water resistance peaks at liftoff speed, so the takeoff is set by the stall speed alone
sol: Below the hump the hull displaces water; past it the floats plane and resistance drops
Seaplanes need a higher thrust to weight ratio to get over the hump

parts.ask: Examiner twist: a conceptual Venus surface version keeps the same mass and wing. Venus surface: ρ = 65 kg/m³, g = 8.87 m/s². Find its liftoff speed at 1.1V_stall.
sol: V_LO = 2.79 m/s, walking pace: the dense atmosphere does the lifting

problems.x: Ground roll grows with W/S over ρC_Lmax and with liftoff ground speed squared, so high lift, headwind and dense air all shorten the takeoff.

problems.title: Trim with a canard versus an aft tail
problems.setup: An aircraft of W = 100 kN has a wing with aerodynamic centre at x = 10.0 m (measured aft of the nose) and wing pitching moment about its AC M_ac = −20 kN·m (nose down). Mean chord c̄ = 4 m. Conventional layout: CG at x = 9.6 m, aft tail AC at x = 22.0 m. Canard layout: same wing, canard AC at x = 2.0 m, wing area 40 m², canard area 8 m², equal lift slopes per unit area, downwash and upwash between surfaces neglected. Lift positive up, nose-up moment positive.

parts.ask: Conventional layout: find the tail lift L_t needed to trim (positive up).
sol: Substituting: −12L_t = 60, so L_t = −5 kN (download) and L_w = 105 kN

parts.ask: Canard layout: find the neutral point x_np.
sol: Neutral point = lift slope weighted centroid of the surfaces
x_np = 8.67 m, ahead of the wing AC

parts.ask: Put the canard layout CG at a 10% static margin. Find the canard trim lift L_c.
Find the ratio of canard C_L to wing C_L in that trim.
sol: C_L ∝ L/S at a common q

parts.ask: Examiner twist: what does that C_L ratio mean for stall?
parts.a: The canard works at a higher C_L and stalls first, so the nose drops and the wing stays below its stall: a built in stall protection that also caps the usable wing C_Lmax
w: The wing stalls first, and the canard then pitches the nose up into a deep stall
Both surfaces reach C_Lmax together because they share the same lift slope
The canard carries a download at stall, like an aft tail, so the wing stalls first
sol: A stable canard sits ahead of the CG with a higher loading
Canard stall unloads the nose, so the wing is held below its own C_Lmax

problems.x: A stable canard trims with an upload and shares the weight with the wing, while a conventional tail usually trims with a download that the wing must carry.
